## What you take with you {#what-you-take-with-you .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **Yours now**: a reproduced result · an estimand statement and a causal graph that you wrote yourself · your results on the class chart, with a reason for each choice
- **Read**: the three *Nature* 2026 papers [@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial; @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness; @TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial] · the glossary [@NosekEtAl2025BriefGlossaryTerms] · @LundbergEtAl2021WhatYourEstimand · on colliders, @ColeEtAl2010IllustratingBiasDue and @GriffithEtAl2020ColliderBiasUndermines · on fixed and random effects, @BellJones2015ExplainingFixedEffects · on reverse causation, @LeszczenskyWolbring2022HowDealReverse · the paper itself [@McLaren2012CulturalDivideEurope]
- **Explore**: the case study, the decision map and the companion modules on the course site · the ESS Data Portal · the SCORE dossier on the OSF
- **Keep going locally**: the research-software and open-research teams at your university · a ReproducibiliTea journal club near you
- Everything is on the course site, and everything is open – fork any of it
:::

::: notes
You take home a reproduced result, an estimand statement and a causal graph that you wrote for a real published claim, and your results on the class chart, each with a reason. The reading list on the slide is short on purpose: the three Nature papers on reproduction, robustness and replication, the glossary that gave us the grid, the paper on estimands, two short papers on what conditioning on a collider does, one on fixed and random effects, one on what panel data can and cannot do about reverse causation, and the original paper. The course site has the case study, the decision map, the companion modules and the full public record. And two pointers for keeping the habit alive: most universities have a research-software team and an open-research or library data service, and ReproducibiliTea journal clubs meet in many cities.
:::
